text: This capstone's three lessons -- provisioning a GPU training cluster, deploying an autoscaling serving endpoint, and a wasted-GPU-spend case study -- pulled on every chapter of this course, not just the ones that sound most directly related. This lesson traces each decision back to the chapter that made it possible, then closes the course.

Chapter 1 is why picking an A100 instance family in Lesson 29 needed no re-explanation, and Chapter 2 is that lesson in full -- Terraform provisioning, driver and CUDA setup, and Kubernetes GPU scheduling, combined into one working cluster. Chapter 3's checkpointing discipline doesn't get its own lesson here, but it's the reason Lesson 31's incident wasted compute instead of losing real training progress.

Chapter 4 is Lesson 30's architecture directly -- the Deployment, Service, Ingress, and GPU-utilization autoscaling metric, combined for the first time with scale-to-zero. Chapter 7 shows up quietly in that same lesson's one deliberate tradeoff: skipping a PodDisruptionBudget on a scale-to-zero endpoint is exactly the availability-versus-cost call its SLO framework asks you to make on purpose.

Chapter 5 draws a distinction worth keeping: infrastructure-level alerting and model-quality monitoring are two different things, and Lesson 31's gap was the former. Chapter 6 is that lesson almost word for word -- the abstract warning that an idle or stalled GPU is a categorically bigger budget problem than an idle CPU VM, made concrete through one stuck thread and four wasted days.

Nothing in these three lessons was a new skill invented for this capstone. Each one took chapters you'd already built separately and put them to work together on one continuous storyline -- provisioning for real, serving for real, and understanding exactly what two specific alerts would have caught in a real cost incident.

AI Cloud Infrastructure, GPU Computing & MLOps is now complete -- one of four Expert Specialization courses in the Cloud Engineer to Cloud Architect path, alongside Advanced Platform Engineering, Hybrid & Multi-Cloud Enterprise Architecture, and Advanced SRE. All four build on the same Advanced Specialization foundation but not on each other, so from here, they can be taken in any order.
